title: The Canonization: title and opening
short: Canonization is the Church's formal declaration of a saint; the lovers will be made saints of love. The opening is an exasperated outburst at a critic.
body: Canonization is the process by which the Roman Catholic Church enrols a person in its 'canon' or list of saints. Donne, raised a Catholic, turns the process into the poem's structure: the lovers renounce the world, suffer and die (in love), have their 'legends' written, and are finally invoked by later lovers as saints. The abrupt opening addresses an unseen friend who has been urging the speaker to give up love for a career. Readers often link the poem's 'ruin'd fortune' to Donne's secret marriage in 1601, which cost him his post with Sir Thomas Egerton.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1
Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Elegies and The Songs and Sonnets (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965), commentary
R. C. Bald, John Donne: A Life (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1970), on the marriage of 1601 and its consequences

anchor: chide my palsie, or my gout
title: palsie ... gout ... five gray haires
short: A mock self-portrait: the critic may scold the speaker's palsy (trembling paralysis), gout and grey hairs, or jeer at his ruined fortunes.
body: 'Palsy' is paralysis or uncontrollable trembling; gout a painful disease of the joints associated with age and rich living. The speaker offers his critic any other target: mock his ailments, his age ('five gray haires', comically precise), or his 'ruin'd fortune' ('flout' = scoff at), so long as he lets him love. The comic exaggeration of age and decay also anticipates the poem's later claim that lovers are above worldly ruin.

Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'flout, v.'
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to ll. 2-3

title: Take you a course ... his honour, or his grace
short: Advice to the critic to pursue a career: a course of action, a place at court, and to pay court to lords and dukes or bishops.
body: A 'course' is a career or line of action; a 'place' is a post or office. 'His honour' and 'his grace' are forms of address for nobles (and, for 'grace', for dukes and archbishops). The lines satirise the courtier's life of observing and flattering great men, exactly the ambition Donne himself pursued in the 1590s and lost by his marriage.

sources.cite: Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to ll. 5-6
Arthur F. Marotti, John Donne, Coterie Poet (Madison: University of Wisconsin Press, 1986)

title: the Kings reall, or his stamped face
short: Contemplate the King's real (royal) face at court, or his face stamped on coins: seek either favour or money. A pun on 'real', a Spanish coin.
body: The critic can gaze on the King's actual face (as a courtier) or on his image stamped on money (as a man of business). 'Reall' sets the actual face against the stamped one, with a play on 'royal' (some also hear the Spanish silver coin, the real). Grierson quotes at length a sermon of Donne's on Caesar's face on coins, which recalls Christ's question about Caesar's image on the tribute money (Matthew 22:20-21).

sources.cite: H. J. C. Grierson (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, 2 vols (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), vol. 2, commentary, note to l. 7, quoting the Sermons
The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Matthew 22:20-21

anchor: So you will let me love.
title: stanza and refrain on 'love'
short: Each nine-line stanza begins and ends with the word 'love', a refrain-like frame that keeps the subject constant while the argument moves.
body: The first line of every stanza ends on 'love', and so does the last, a short line that varies a formula: 'So you will let me love', 'Though she and I do love', 'Mysterious by this love', 'Us Canoniz'd for Love', 'A patterne of our love'. The progression traces the poem's argument from defence, through mystery, to canonization. The stanza, rhymed abbacccaa with the last line shortened, is again Donne's own design.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1
Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Elegies and The Songs and Sonnets (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965), introduction, on stanza forms
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), headnote

title: merchants ships ... sighs drown'd
short: A parody of Petrarchan hyperbole: his sighs have not raised storms, nor his tears caused floods, nor his chills delayed the spring.
body: Petrarchan lovers routinely claimed that their sighs were tempests, their tears floods, and their alternating fever and chill (the 'icy fire' of love) affected the weather. Donne takes these conventions literally to show that his love harms nobody's trade, land or harvest. 'Forward spring' is an early spring; 'remove' means put back. The joke turns a defence of private love into a satire on the inflated language of love poetry.

sources.cite: Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Elegies and The Songs and Sonnets (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965), commentary
Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1

title: the plaguie Bill
short: The weekly Bill of Mortality listing deaths in London, especially from plague: his feverish passion has killed no one.
body: London parishes published weekly 'bills of mortality' recording burials and causes of death, issued regularly during epidemics, and continuously from the great plague of 1603. The 'heats' in his veins (the fever of love) have not added a single plague death to the list. The detail gives the poem a sharp topical texture: real deaths in the city are set against the lover's metaphorical sickness.

title: Soldiers ... Lawyers ... Litigious men
short: Soldiers and lawyers will still find wars and lawsuits; the world's business goes on whether the lovers love or not.
body: The stanza's argument concludes that the lovers harm no one: soldiers still find wars, lawyers still find quarrelsome clients ('Litigious men' who 'move' or start quarrels). Donne, a former student at Lincoln's Inn and soldier on the Cadiz and Islands expeditions (1596-7), knew both worlds. The satire implies the public world is itself driven by conflict, against which private love is innocent.

sources.cite: R. C. Bald, John Donne: A Life (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1970), on Lincoln's Inn and the expeditions of 1596-7
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to ll. 16-17

title: flye ... Tapers ... die
short: Call them flies (moths drawn to a flame) or candles that burn themselves out; 'die' carries the common sexual pun on orgasm.
body: The lovers accept any name. A 'flye' may be a moth that flies into a candle and is destroyed; they are also 'Tapers' (candles) consuming themselves. 'Die' was a common Elizabethan pun on sexual climax, and a popular belief held that each act of love shortened life, hence 'at our owne cost'. Brooks takes this cluster as an example of how Donne's paradoxes fuse the sacred and the sexual.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1

title: the Eagle and the dove
short: Strength and gentleness (or male and female) combined; both birds also had religious and alchemical meanings.
body: The eagle stood for strength, masculinity and royalty, the dove for meekness, femininity and peace (and the Holy Spirit). The lovers contain both. Some critics also read both as alchemical symbols for stages in the transmutation of matter, which leads into the alchemical-sounding 'neutrall thing' and the Phoenix. Critics differ over how far to press the alchemical reading; Brooks emphasises the paradox of opposites united.

anchor: The Phoenix ridle hath more wit
title: The Phoenix ridle
short: The fabled phoenix, a single bird that burns itself and rises from its ashes; the lovers solve its riddle by being two who are one.
body: The phoenix of classical legend (described by Pliny, Natural History 10.2, and in Lactantius' poem De ave phoenice) is unique, without a mate, and periodically dies in flames to be reborn from its ashes. Its 'riddle' is how one bird could reproduce itself. The lovers, 'two being one', make the riddle meaningful: they are the phoenix, dying and rising 'the same'. The phoenix was also a Christian emblem of resurrection.

sources.cite: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 10.2

title: one neutrall thing
short: The two sexes combine into one sexless or two-sexed being; editors disagree whether the line ends the Phoenix sentence or begins the next.
body: 'Neutral' means of neither sex (as in grammar), suggesting an androgynous union like Plato's original double humans in the Symposium, or the alchemical hermaphrodite. Grierson argued from manuscript punctuation that the line must go with what follows: both sexes fit so entirely into one neutral thing 'that' we die and rise the same. Chambers and others link it with the preceding Phoenix lines. The archive's comma after 'So' follows the 1633 edition.

sources.cite: H. J. C. Grierson (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, 2 vols (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), vol. 2, commentary, note to ll. 24-5
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to l. 25
Plato, Symposium 189c-193d (speech of Aristophanes)

anchor: Wee dye and rise the same
title: Wee dye and rise the same ... Mysterious
short: Sexual 'death' and recovery, phoenix rebirth and Christian resurrection fused in one phrase; their love is a sacred 'mystery'.
body: The lovers 'die' in sexual consummation and 'rise' unchanged, like the phoenix and, blasphemously, like Christ or the faithful at the resurrection. 'Mysterious' carries the religious sense of a 'mystery', a truth beyond reason revealed only to initiates, as in the sacraments. Brooks made this stanza central to his argument that the language of poetry is the language of paradox.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'mystery, n.1'
Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Elegies and The Songs and Sonnets (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965), commentary

title: tombes and hearse ... legends ... Chronicle
short: If their story is not fit for funeral monuments or history ('Chronicle'), it will do for poetry; 'legends' are saints' lives.
body: A 'legend' was originally the life of a saint, read aloud (Latin legenda), as in the medieval Golden Legend. A 'hearse' was the frame over a coffin on which verses and epitaphs were pinned. 'Chronicle' is official history. The lovers will not be commemorated in public monuments or histories, but verse will serve as their legend, preparing their canonization. The poem itself becomes the saints' legend, the written evidence of their holy life.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'legend, n.'
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'hearse, n.'
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to ll. 29-31

anchor: We'll build in sonnets pretty roomes
title: sonnets pretty roomes
short: A pun: the Italian 'stanza' means 'room'; their monument will be built of stanzas. 'Sonnets' means love poems generally.
body: In Donne's time 'sonnet' could mean any short love lyric, not only the fourteen-line form (the collection of his lyrics printed in 1633 is called Songs and Sonets, though it contains few sonnets). 'Pretty roomes' plays on the Italian stanza ('room, stopping-place'), so the poem is itself the chapel or tomb in which the lovers are enshrined. The idea that verse outlasts monuments goes back to Horace (Odes 3.30, 'exegi monumentum').

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'stanza, n.'
Horace, Odes 3.30

title: a well wrought urne
short: A finely made urn suits great ashes as well as vast tombs: the small poem holds the lovers worthily. The phrase gave Cleanth Brooks his book title.
body: A cinerary urn, holding the ashes of the dead, is set against 'halfe-acre tombes', the enormous monuments of the great. The small, carefully made object honours its contents as well as any grand tomb, as the lyric honours the lovers. Cleanth Brooks took the phrase as the title of The Well Wrought Urn (1947), the classic New Critical study, where he reads the poem itself as such an urn, a self-contained structure of paradox.

sources.cite: Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1
Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Elegies and The Songs and Sonnets (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965), commentary

title: hymnes ... Canoniz'd
short: The poems become hymns, sacred songs, and readers' approval is the act that canonizes the lovers.
body: The 'sonnets' of l. 32 have become 'hymnes', songs of praise for saints. 'Approve' means to confirm or attest, as in a formal process of canonization, where evidence of sanctity is approved. The stanza thus completes the analogy: renunciation, death, legend, and now official recognition of the lovers as saints of love. All who read the hymns become witnesses in the cause.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'approve, v.1'
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to ll. 35-6

title: And thus invoke us
short: Future lovers will pray to them as saints, asking them to intercede; Grierson notes Donne's precise use of the doctrine of saints' intercession.
body: Catholic practice invokes saints, asking them to pray to God for the petitioner. Grierson observes that Donne is 'pedantically accurate' here: later lovers ask the canonized pair to 'beg from above' a pattern of love for them. The Protestant Church of England rejected the invocation of saints, so the conceit has a daring, even provocative edge given Donne's Catholic background.

sources.cite: H. J. C. Grierson (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, 2 vols (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), vol. 2, commentary, note to ll. 37-45
Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Elegies and The Songs and Sonnets (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1965), commentary
John Carey, John Donne: Life, Mind and Art (London: Faber, 1981), on Donne's apostasy

title: one anothers hermitage
short: Each lover was the other's place of retreat from the world, as a hermit's cell; love once 'peace' is now the world's 'rage'.
body: A hermitage is the solitary dwelling of a religious recluse. The lovers withdrew from the world into each other, as hermits withdraw to the desert. The line 'You, to whom love was peace, that now is rage' is not easy to read; it seems to set the calm of the canonized lovers against the turbulence ('rage') of love for those who now invoke them. The monastic image continues the poem's sacred vocabulary.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'hermitage, n.'
Cleanth Brooks, 'The Language of Paradox', in The Well Wrought Urn: Studies in the Structure of Poetry (New York: Reynal & Hitchcock, 1947), ch. 1

anchor: Into the glasses of your eyes
title: contract ... glasses of your eyes
short: The lovers drew the soul of the whole world into their eyes, which became mirrors and 'spies' summarising all countries, towns and courts.
body: Grierson defends 'contract' against the manuscript variant 'extract', and explains that the object of 'drove' is 'Countries, Townes, Courts': the lovers compressed the world's essence and drove it into each other's eyes, which reflect it in miniature like mirrors or optical 'perspective' glasses. 'Epitomize' means to sum up in brief. The image is the same microcosm as 'The Sunne Rising', where the world is 'contracted' into the lovers.

sources.cite: H. J. C. Grierson (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, 2 vols (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), vol. 2, commentary, note to ll. 37-45 and l. 40
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'epitomize, v.'
Robin Robbins (ed.), The Poems of John Donne, Longman Annotated English Poets, 2 vols (Harlow: Pearson Longman, 2008), note to ll. 40-44

title: Beg frow above / A patterne of our love
short: A textual crux: the 1633 edition reads 'our love', which the archive follows; Grierson argued for the manuscript reading 'your love'.
body: Grierson prints 'your love', arguing that 'Beg' is an imperative addressed by future lovers to the canonized pair ('You whom reverend love ...'): they ask the saints to obtain from heaven a pattern of 'your' love, the saints' love, as a model for themselves. The 1633 reading 'our love' would then be a copyist's error, though it can be read as 'a pattern for our love'. Modern editors are divided. 'Frow' in the archive text is a misprint for 'from'. 'Patterne' means exemplar, model to copy.
